betterCitation: Nishida Kitarō, An Inquiry into the Good, Part I, ch. 1, the opening sentence, p. 3 (trans. Masao Abe and Christopher Ives, 1990)
reason: Refuted, because the correction the verifier made is the thing that breaks it. The card would ship To experience means to know facts just as they are. with a full stop, and calls that the opening sentence. Every witness I could reach prints the opening sentence running on past a comma: To experience means to know facts just as they are, to know in accordance with facts by completely relinquishing one's own fabrications. I got that comma form three times from three different pages, the Kyoto School of Philosophy quotations page the verifier itself used, a Buddhism reading page, and an essay reprinted at Open Horizons, all three citing An Inquiry into the Good, 3. Not one witness anywhere prints a full stop after they are. So the stop on the card is the card's own, and the trim turns a clause into a sentence the book does not contain. That is minting wording, which rule 12 forbids outright, and it is worse than a paraphrase because it is invisible: the line reads as a complete Nishida sentence and no reader could tell it had been cut. The source line makes the same claim in words, opening sentence, which is false of the text as trimmed. I tried hard to get the Yale page itself and could not, and that failure is the second half of the refutation. The Abe and Ives volume is on archive.org as inquiryintogood0000nish, 1990, but it is a lending item: the search-inside endpoint returns nothing and the djvu text returns 403. Wikipedia's article on the work quotes no text at all. The one scholarly article that would settle it, the De Gruyter piece on Nishida's experience theory, refuses automated fetches. So the translator attribution rests entirely on secondary pages, and none of the three that print the sentence names a translator: they cite only An Inquiry into the Good, 3. The card names Abe and Ives as the source of its wording, and that is an inference from the title and the page number, not something I or the verifier read. It is probably right, since An Inquiry into the Good is the Yale title and Viglielmo's 1960 rendering of the same book is titled A Study of Good, but probably right is not this track's standard, and the two translations are known to open in very similar English, which is exactly the trap. The rest is sound and I want it on the record, because the line deserves to ship in its real form. Nishida is not banned, not at cap, at zero for the year, appears nowhere in carry.json and nowhere else in June. shipped.js is clean on the trimmed line and clean on the full sentence too, which I also ran. Zen no kenkyu is 1911 and the translation 1990, so the pre-2000 rule is met twice over. Philosophy is the form. The theme fit is exact and is the best argument for rescuing it: knowing facts just as they are is June's sentence. The fix is to ship the whole opening sentence, which every witness attests: To experience means to know facts just as they are, to know in accordance with facts by completely relinquishing one's own fabrications. That is 136 characters with the curly apostrophe, it ends in the source's own full stop, and the better citation above is 129 characters, leads with the name and carries no dash. If the editor will not carry a hedge on the translator, the note must say plainly that the wording is the one every witness prints for page 3 of the English An Inquiry into the Good and that the Yale page was not opened.

residual: The Yale volume is still unopened, and the archive.org copy is locked. If it can be opened, two things settle at once: whether Abe and Ives is the right translator for this English, and whether the sentence really ends after fabrications. Until then the line should ship whole, with a note that says what is and is not known, rather than trimmed with a stop that nobody has seen in print.
